activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Naomi sat on the playroom rug. She wanted to build a tower of blocks. But she was thirsty first. She drank water from her little cup.

Then she saw a ball. She gave it a push. The ball rolled away. "Why did it roll?" she asked.

Naomi picked up a square block. She pushed it on the rug. The block did not roll. It just slid and stopped.

She picked up the ball again. It was round all over, like a circle. She pushed it. Round things roll.

So she stacked square blocks and triangle blocks and rectangle blocks for her tower. They stayed put. At the top she put nothing round.

"Square blocks can't roll away," said Naomi. "So I win. My tower is safe."

Her tummy growled. "Snack time," said Mama from the door. Naomi ran to the table. She picked up her fork. She looked at it. "My fork has squares on the handle," she said. "Good. It won't roll off my plate."

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Wyatt stood at the bus stop with Mama. The sun was out. "Sunny today," said Wyatt. He wore his big sun hat. The wind came. It went whoosh. His hat flew off his head. "Come back, hat!" said Wyatt.

Mama laughed. She picked up the hat. "The wind pushed it," she said. Wyatt put the hat back on. He held it with both hands. "I hold it," said Wyatt. "The wind can't get it!" The wind went whoosh again. The hat stayed on. "Ha!" said Wyatt.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell. Drip, drop. Wyatt was warm. He had his raincoat on. He zipped it up to his chin. "Rainy, rainy," said Wyatt. The bus came. He climbed the steps. "Bye bye, wind!" he said. The wind went whoosh.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: counting, comparing amounts, and shapes
fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
story:
Grandma poured two bowls of strawberries. One bowl was red and big. One bowl was small. "Which bowl has more?" Grandma asked.

Sarah looked and looked. She could not tell. So she counted. She touched each berry. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." The big bowl had seven.

The cat came by. Its paws were dirty, so Grandma said, "Cat, go outside." The cat sat by the door and waited.

Sarah counted the small bowl. She started with the berry on top. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted again. This time she started with the berry at the bottom. "One, two, three, four, five." Still five!

"Grandma! I counted that way, and I counted this way," Sarah said. "Both times, the last number was five."

Grandma smiled. "So which bowl has more?"

"The big bowl has seven. Seven is more than five."

Sarah ate her seven berries, one by one. "One, two, three," she said, and she kept counting to the very last one.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Brielle got to school early. It was writing time. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

She grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The B came out big and fat. The letters ran into each other. "Oh no," said Brielle. "My name looks like a blob."

Her friend Milo laughed, but not a mean laugh. It was a silly joke about the blob. Then he showed her his hand. He held his pencil near the tip. He used just two fingers and his thumb, like a little pinch.

Brielle tried the pinch. She held the pencil near the tip too. She wrote B, then R, then I. She stopped to count the letters left. E, L, L, E. She wrote them one at a time.

"Look!" said Brielle. "When I pinch the pencil, my letters come out small and neat." She held up her paper. Her name was all there.

"Nice writing," said Milo.

"I will write it again," said Brielle. She pinched the pencil and began the B.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Charlotte went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a cat. Cats were her favorite.

The picture books sat in big bins. Each bin had a label. One bin said animals. One bin said toys. One bin said foods.

Charlotte looked in the animals bin. She found a book about a dog. She found a book about a fish. But no cat book.

Then she looked in the toys bin. There was a book about a cow. A cow was not a toy! A cow was an animal, like a cat. So the cow book was in the wrong bin. That is why she could not find it. Maybe someone had mixed the bins up.

A cart rolled by with a squeaky wheel. The librarian stopped and smiled. "That book looks silly sitting there," she said.

"I can fix it," said Charlotte. She put the cow book in the animals bin. Then she looked again. Under the dog book was a cat book!

"Found it!" she did not yell, but she wanted to.

She sat down with her dad. The cat in the book chased a ball of yarn.

"Is yarn a toy?" Charlotte wondered. She turned the page to see.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Mila sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her curly hair was in two little puffs. Today she had to get a shot in her arm. She did not want a shot. She held her arm stiff and tight, like a wooden stick.

The nurse came in with a small tray. "Can you hold still for me?" she asked. Mila squeezed her arm even tighter. It felt hard as a rock. The nurse shook her head. "A tight arm makes the shot hurt more," she said. "A soft, floppy arm helps it hurt less."

Mila looked at her arm. She let her shoulder go soft. She let her arm droop down, loose and floppy like a noodle. "Okay," she said. "My arm is soft now."

The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Mila blinked. "That was small," she said. Then she got a bright bandage with stars on it.

On the way out, Mila did not hurry. She held her sticker up to the light. "Soft arm, small pinch," she told her mama. "See my stars?"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Lennon went to the store with Dad today. Yesterday they had no bananas left. So today they would get more.

"Look," said Dad. "This banana is green."

"Can we eat it now?" asked Lennon.

"Not now. Green means later," said Dad. "It turns yellow later. Then we can eat it tomorrow."

Lennon held the green banana. It felt hard. She put it in the cart, next to a small toy mouse. She made the mouse whisper, "Wait, banana, wait."

Then Lennon's legs felt weak from walking. Dad saw her rubbing her eyes. He picked her up. "You need help now," he said. "Rest now, walk later."

At home, Lennon put the banana on the window sill. "Tomorrow you will be yellow," she whispered.

The next morning, the banana was yellow. "It changed because I waited!" said Lennon.

Dad peeled it. Lennon took a big bite. "Today it is ready," she said. "Today is the best day."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Ayla sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted the green sticker on the wall. But first she had to wait.

The room had balloons. They floated up by the roof. One floated down to Ayla. She touched it with her hands. It felt smooth and cool.

The doctor came in. "Look here," he said. He held up a card with grass on it. Ayla used her eyes to see it. Then she covered her eyes with her hands. Now she could not see the grass! She moved her hands away. She could see it again. "My eyes make me see," said Ayla.

The doctor tickled her toes. Her skin felt the tickle. He shook a little bell. Ayla heard it with her ears. She held her nose closed. She tried to smell the sweet orange the doctor held out. She could not smell it. She let go of her nose. Mmm, now she could! She took a tiny taste with her tongue. Sour and sweet.

Then Ayla got mad because the visit was over. The doctor gave her the green sticker. She put it on her shirt. "Thank you," she said. The balloons floated up, and Ayla waved bye-bye to them.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Mateo ran into Grandma's house. "Where is the baby?" he asked. Grandma pointed to a soft blue blanket. A tiny baby was inside. "That is your new brother," said Grandma.

Mateo wanted the baby to laugh. He poked the baby's tummy. The baby did not laugh. The baby made a small frown. Mateo tried again. Still no laugh. He felt sad.

Grandpa held up the baby's little hand. Mateo put one finger near it. He tickled the tiny palm. The baby grabbed Mateo's finger and held on tight. The baby made a small smile. "Grandpa, look!" said Mateo. "I tickle his hand, and he holds me!"

Grandma laughed. "Babies love to grab fingers," she said. Mateo wiggled his finger. The baby held on and on. Then Mateo gave the baby a cold spoon from a glass of water on the table. The baby grabbed that too.

"He can hold everything," said Mateo. "Not me," said Grandpa, holding up his big hand. "Too big!" Mateo laughed. The baby squeezed his finger again, like a tiny hello.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Leah had a new swimsuit. It had a scratchy tag. Mom said, "I will cut the tag off." Snip, snip went the scissors. Now the suit felt smooth.

Leah sat on the wood bench in the changing room. The room was quiet after her swim class. She shivered. Her legs were wet. Why was she so cold? She looked down. Water sat on her skin like little beads. "Maybe the water makes me cold," she said. She picked up her big towel. She patted her arms. She patted her legs. She patted her hair too.

The water went into the towel. Her skin was dry now. The shivering stopped. "Mom, look! The water went away, and I am warm!" Mom smiled. Then Leah pulled on her socks. One sock had a hole. Her toe popped out and said, "Hello!"

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Hudson stood in the big school gym. He had a red beanbag in his hand. On the floor was a hoop. He wanted to get the beanbag in it.

He threw the beanbag very low. It slid along the floor and missed. The beanbag made a soft sound on the wood.

Hudson tried again. He held his arm up high. He let go up high, not down low. The beanbag flew up and dropped into the hoop. "I did it!" said Hudson.

Then Coach Maya rolled him a big blue ball. It hit his tummy and fell. His hands were too far apart. "Why did it fall?" Hudson asked. "My hands were messy, all over." He put his two hands close together. He made a big bowl with them. Coach Maya rolled the ball again. Hudson caught it and held it tight.

"I can show you," Hudson said to his friend Ben. He held his arm up high. The beanbag went in the hoop. Ben clapped his hands.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Asher ran to the big slide. His tummy felt bouncy and jumpy. "I am so excited!" he said. He wanted to slide down all by himself.

He climbed up the ladder. It was very tall. Then he looked down. His legs felt wobbly. "I'm scared," he whispered. He sat at the top and did not move.

A girl named Mia climbed up too. "Want to go together?" she asked. Asher nodded. Mia went first. Asher held the sides and went slow. Whee! He slid down and landed in the soft sand. "I did it!" he laughed. His mouth made a big smile. He felt happy.

But then a big boy ran by and bumped him. Asher fell down in the sand. His face got hot and scrunched up. "That made me angry!" he said. Mia helped him stand. Then Asher spun in a circle, round and round, until he felt dizzy and fell laughing into the sand.

The big boy came back. He looked down and his eyes were watery. "I fell too," he said. "I feel sad." Asher patted his arm. "Come spin with us," he said. "Spinning makes me laugh." So they all spun in one big circle, round and round, until they toppled over together in the sand.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Adam had a library book about trucks. He loved it so much. He wanted to keep it forever.

At bedtime, Dad said, "Time for your book." Adam opened the front cover. The pages went one way, to the back. Dad pointed at the little marks on the page. "Those are words," he said. "They tell the story." Adam traced a word with his finger. "The words say truck!" he said.

Then Dad said, "We must take the book back on Friday." Adam held the book tight. "Why?" he asked. "Other kids want to read it too," said Dad.

Outside, a soft storm was starting. Rain tapped the window. Adam smelled his dog's stinky paws on the blanket. He giggled.

"I will not forget Friday," Adam said. He put the book by the door. Then he snuggled down. The rain went tap, tap, tap.

"Good night, truck book," Adam whispered.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Ethan ran up to the bookmobile. It was a little truck full of books. The librarian smiled. "Would you like your own library card?" Ethan nodded big. She wrote his name on a small blue card. Ethan held it with both hands.

Then he found a book about a squishy red tomato. He hugged it tight. "This book is mine now," he said. The librarian shook her head. "You can take it home. But you must bring it back so other kids can read it too." Ethan looked sad. Then he looked at the tomato book. "Okay," he said. "But just for a little while."

At lunch, Ethan showed the tomato book to Mama. He put the book on the table. It sat by his cheese. After lunch he read it three times. That night, the book went under his blanket. Tomorrow he would read it again. Soon he would bring it back. Then he would get a new one. Ethan patted the cover and whispered, "Good night, tomato."

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Maya ran to the park with her bear, Brown. She loved the park so much. Today she would play house under the big tree.

A boy nearby threw a paper plane. It zoomed up and glided down. "Again!" Maya shouted. Then she set up her house. A flat stone would be the table. A leaf would be the bed for Brown.

Maya laid Brown on the leaf. But the leaf was bumpy. Brown rolled off. Thump! Brown fell in the grass. Maya tried again. Brown rolled off again.

She looked at the leaf. It was not flat. The bumpy parts pushed Brown right off. "The bed is too bumpy," Maya said. So she found a smooth, flat leaf. She patted the dirt under it. She laid Brown down. Brown stayed put. Maya clapped.

Then she found a small stick. It became a spoon. She stirred dirt and water. "Soup for Brown!" she said. The soup was warm from the sun.

The paper plane came gliding back. It landed right by the leaf bed. Maya laughed. "Brown, you have a new friend!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Hayden sat at the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint. He looked and looked. Red, blue, yellow. Red, blue, yellow. No green.

Then Leo came over. Leo was grumpy because he had no red paint. Hayden had lots of red paint. He pushed his red cup over to Leo. Leo smiled and said, "Thank you."

Hayden was still stuck. He dipped his brush in blue. He painted a blue frog. Then he dipped the brush in yellow too. The blue and yellow mixed on the paper. The frog turned green!

"Blue and yellow make green," said Hayden.

Miss Ana helped him hang the frog by the window. The sun made the wet paint shine. Then Miss Ana let him pet the class pet, a soft brown bunny. "Nice green frog," said Leo.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Paisley stood in the restaurant kitchen with her grandma. A big chef hat was too big, so grandma let her wear a small one instead. On the counter sat warm toast, soft butter, and a cup.

"Can I do the butter?" Paisley asked. Grandma cut a tiny piece of butter and put it on the knife. Paisley pressed hard. The butter ripped a hole in the toast. A little piece fell to the floor. "Oh no," said Paisley.

"Try again," said grandma. She set out a new slice of warm toast. Paisley slid the knife slow and soft this time. The butter went on like paint. "Gentle hands work," said Paisley.

Next came the milk. The jug was heavy. Paisley lifted it high and the milk splashed out of the cup. A white puddle grew on the counter. She felt a little lost. Grandma held her hand around the jug. "Tip it slowly," said grandma. Paisley tipped it just a little. The milk slid down the side of the cup and filled it up. "Slow tipping makes no splash," said Paisley.

Grandma wiped the puddle with a cloth. Through the window, Paisley saw a tree in the sun. They sat on two stools and ate the toast and drank the milk together.

"Mmm," said grandma. "Best toast in town."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Clara ran to the water table at school. "Look, a big boat!" she said. She put it in the water. It went slow. Then Sam came with a small boat. His boat went fast! "Why is yours fast?" Clara asked.

Sam pushed his boat again. "My boat is small," he said. "Small boats go fast." Clara tried her big boat. It went slow, slow, slow. She wanted a fast boat too.

Then Clara had an idea. She took the small boat and put the big boat on top. "Now they go together!" she said. Sam pushed hard. The big boat went fast with the small boat on its back. "Look, look!" said Clara.

Teacher Mia brought warm cocoa for snack. Clara touched her cup. "Hot," she said, and blew on it. Then she took a big drink. "Now it's cold enough!" After snack, Clara sat down to draw an ocean with two fast boats on it. "This one is big," she said, pointing. "This one is small." Sam yawned, all sleepy. Clara drew a bed for him in the picture, right next to the ocean.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Violet put on her new swimsuit. It was blue with white dots. Dad drove her to the pool by the lake. The lake water was far away. The pool water was close and blue.

Violet stood on the step. "I want to swim," she said. "But water goes in my nose." Dad held her hand. "Watch me," he said. He put his mouth in the water. He blew out. Bubbles came up. Bloop, bloop, bloop.

Violet tried it. She put her mouth near the water. She blew out. Bubbles came from her lips. No water went in her nose. She blew bubbles again and again. Then she kicked her feet. Dad held her tummy. The bubbles came up, and she did not cough. "Blowing keeps the water out," Violet said.

They sat by the pool in the warm light. Violet took a big bite of her apple. Dad wrapped her in a soft towel. "Swim again tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Violet. "Bubbles first."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Amelia wanted to make a ice cube last all day at school. She put one big ice cube and one tiny ice cube in her cup. The tiny one was as small as a mouse. "Which one will melt first?" she asked her friend Tom.

At play time, they ran to look. The tiny cube was gone. The big cube was still there. Amelia clapped her hands. "The small one melted fast," she said. "The big one melts slow."

The sun was hot on the shelf. So Amelia moved the cup to a cold spot near the window shade. Tom watched with wide eyes. "Will the big one melt now?" he asked.

Amelia waited and watched. The big ice cube sat still. It did not melt. "It melts slow because it is big," she said. "And it is cold here, not hot." The water in the cup did not grow one bit.

At tidy up time, Amelia put her cup in the sink. The big ice cube was still there, small now, but not gone. "You can come to my house," she told the ice cube. Tom laughed. "You talk to ice!" he said. Amelia giggled and waved the cup goodbye.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Weston saw a big table at the festival. There was warm bread on it. He wanted some right now. He grabbed a piece, but Grandma held his hand.

"Not yet," she said. "First we say our family greeting. We hold hands. We say it together. Then we eat."

Weston pouted. His tummy made a growly sound. But he took Grandma's hand anyway. He took Papa's hand too. Everyone made a big circle, like a cloud around the table.

Grandma started the greeting. Weston listened. Then he said the words too, loud and silly. "Good bread, good friends, good day!"

Then everyone laughed and picked up bread. Weston took a big bite. "It is salty!" he said, with his mouth full.

Grandma smiled. "You said it with us. Now the bread tastes even better."

Weston looked around. "Everyone eats after we all say it. That is why we hold hands!"

"Yes," said Papa. "One big word, one big bite."

Weston licked his fingers. "Can we do it again? I want more bread."

"First, the greeting," said Grandma, and she held out her hand.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The room went dark. Sienna held Mama's hand tight. "It's too dark," she said.

Mama got her phone. She tapped the back of it. A little light came on. Sienna looked and looked. Then she said, "The light comes on because you tap it." Mama smiled. "Yes. Let's keep it on."

They walked to the kitchen. Sienna's hands were wet from washing them. She wiped them on her towel. Then she tapped the phone too. The light got brighter. It made a circle on the wall.

They made a tent with a big plastic sheet. They sat inside it. The little light shone on the plastic. It looked like a star. Sienna yawned. The rain tapped the window outside. The phone light stayed on, small and warm. "Night night, light," Sienna whispered.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Lincoln was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home today. Her name was Ivy.

Grandma had baked bread. Lincoln could smell it. "Yum," he said. The bread was warm and squishy. He pressed it with his finger. It popped back up.

Then the car came. Daddy carried Ivy inside. She was tiny. She had a little red face. Then Ivy began to cry. "Waa, waa."

"Why is she crying?" Lincoln asked. Grandma held Ivy close. "Let's see. Is her sock too tight? No. Does she need a burp?" Grandma patted her back softly. Burp! Ivy kept crying.

"Is she hungry?" Lincoln asked. Grandma said, "Let's try." Mommy gave Ivy milk. Ivy drank and drank. The crying stopped. Ivy went to sleep.

"She cried because she was hungry," Lincoln said. He counted her tiny toes. One, two, three, four, five. One, two, three, four, five. Ivy slept and slept.

Lincoln gave her a soft pat on her head. "I will help feed you," he whispered.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Nicholas sat on his bed. He had a library book about bears. He loved the bears so much. He wanted to keep the book forever.

He looked at the front cover. There were little marks on it. "Mama, what are these?" he asked. Mama said, "Those are words. They say Bear Book." Nicholas tapped the words. Words could talk! He turned the pages one by one, front to back. The bears went for a swim. Then they went to sleep. "What comes next?" he wondered.

Then Nicholas put the book under his pillow. "Now it is mine," he said. But the next day, Mama came in. "That book is from the library," she said. "We borrowed it. We must take it back so other kids can read it too." Nicholas made a sad face. His tummy felt tight, like a hurt.

Nicholas tried to hide the book in the bath toy box. That was wrong. Books do not like baths! Mama found it just in time. It was dry and safe.

So Nicholas made a plan. He asked, "Can we bring it back and borrow it again?" Mama smiled. "Yes, we can borrow it another day." Nicholas hugged the book one more time. He said, "Bye bye, bears. See you soon." Then he put it in the bag all by himself.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Eloise stood by her bed. The room was dark. She heard a noise. Thump, thump. Eloise began to freeze. Her legs would not move. "Something is under my bed," she whispered. Her tummy felt funny. She was scared.

"Mama!" she called. Mama came in fast. She knelt down by the table and looked under the bed. She pulled out a shoe. Then she pulled out a book. The big book had fallen down. That was the thump. "The book made the noise," Mama said. "The dark makes big noises feel scary." Eloise looked at the book. Her scared feeling got small. A happy feeling grew big.

Mama turned on the little lamp. The room was warm and bright. Eloise was not sad anymore. She hugged her bear tight. "Book go night-night," she said. Mama laughed and kissed her head.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Harrison went to the library with Dad. He wanted a book about dogs. "Where do dog books live?" he asked. "Let's look slowly," said Dad. "We will find one."

They walked past a big shelf. The books there were about food. Apples, bread, and milk. "Not dogs," said Harrison. They walked past another shelf. Those books were about toys. Balls, blocks, and drums. "Not dogs," said Harrison. They tried one more shelf. Those books were about animals. Cats, ducks, cows, and, yes, dogs!

"The dog books live with the animals," said Harrison. "Dogs are animals, so they are here." He pulled out a black book with a big yellow dog on it. He sat down on the soft rug. He turned the pages, one by one. Dad sat close and waited.

Then Harrison made a dog sound. "Woof, woof," he said, very quiet. He tried the page again. The woofs worked. A girl on the rug looked up and smiled. Harrison held the book out to her and said, "Look. A dog. Woof, woof."

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Anna held her daddy's hand. The big yellow bus stopped in front of her. The door opened with a whoosh.

Anna climbed the steps. She looked for a seat. "I want the window seat," she said. A boy named Sam sat by the window. "Can I sit with you?" she asked. "Yes," said Sam. "I like to look out too."

Anna looked out the window. She saw a plane up in the sky. "The plane is so fast!" she said. "It goes fast because it has big wings," said Sam. "Wings go whoosh." Anna laughed. "Whoosh!" she said. "My arms are little wings." She flapped her arms like a bird. Sam laughed too.

The bus went bump, bump, down the road. It stopped again. A new girl got on. Anna waved. "Sit here!" she said. "We can look for planes."

At school, the teacher said, "We will paint today." Anna painted a big yellow bus. She painted a plane above it. "That is my bus," she said. "And that is my plane. I am so smart!" The teacher smiled. Anna smiled too. Then she painted one more thing. It was Sam, waving out the window.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Myles sat on his bed with his library book. It was a book about a big red truck. He wanted to keep it forever. "My book," he said. "Mine forever."

Myles turned the pages. He started at the front. He went to the back. "Books go front to back," he said. He saw little marks on the page. His big sister Rosa read them out loud. "Those marks are words," she said. "The words say what happens."

Then Rosa pointed at a paper slip in the book. It had a day on it. "The book goes back on that day," she said. "Other kids want to read it too." Myles held the book tight. He did not want to give it back.

The next day Rosa helped him wrap the book in a fresh paper bag. It was clean and new. Myles carried it to the library. He set it on the desk. "Book goes back," he said. The librarian smiled. "You can borrow a new one," she said. Myles picked a book about a dog that likes to chew bones. He hugged it. "Front to back," he said, and turned the first page.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Luca stood at the bus stop with Mama. He was ready to go see Grandma. The sun came out. It was sunny and warm. Luca pulled off his hat. "Too hot," he said.

Then the wind came. It was windy. The wind grabbed Luca's hat. The hat flew up in the air. Luca reached and reached. "My hat!" he called. Mama held his hand tight. A kind man caught the hat. "Here you go," he said. Luca put the hat back on. He held it with both hands. "The wind took it because it was light," Luca said.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. It was rainy. Mama opened her big umbrella. Luca stood under it. The rain tapped on top. Tap, tap, tap. Luca stayed dry. He did not get wet at all. "The umbrella stops the rain," Luca said. Mama smiled and nodded.

Luca chewed his little cracker while they waited. He watched a puddle grow by his boots. "In spring we get lots of rain," Mama said. "Rain helps the flowers grow."

The bus came at last. Luca held Mama's hand. They climbed the steps together. Luca waved to the man with the hat. "Bye bye, rainy day!" he said.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Sofia stood by the tent with her small red bag. "What goes in the bag?" she asked. Mom knelt down beside her. "We pack a bag for a trip," Mom said. "Why?" asked Sofia. "Because we cannot use our things at home when we are far away."

Sofia put in her bunny and her socks. She wiggled her hand into her mitten. The mitten felt loose. "It is too big now," she said. "Your hand grew this year," said Mom. Sofia looked and looked. Her fingers went all the way to the end last summer. Now the mitten slipped off when she waved.

At the campsite, Sofia found a big flat stone. She sat on it and pretended the stone was a boat. "Row, row," she said. A wind came through the trees. The leaves shivered. The tent wall puffed out like a balloon. "Why does the tent move?" Sofia asked. Dad smiled. "The wind pushes it," he said. Sofia held up her hand. The wind pushed her fingers back. "The wind pushed me too!" she said. She pushed the tent wall with her palm, and it puffed out the other way. "Now I pushed the tent," she said, and she did it again.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Iris went to the pharmacy with her dad. The pharmacy sold soap, and Iris saw a pink bottle. "Can we buy it?" she asked. Dad said yes.

But there was a rule at preschool. You must wash your hands with soap for twenty seconds. Iris did not know how long twenty seconds was. At snack time, she washed fast, like a bunny hop. Then she ate her crackers.

The next day, her tummy felt bad. She had to stay home. "My hands were not clean," she said. "I washed too fast."

Her teacher sang a hand song. It took twenty seconds to sing. Iris sang it while she washed, all the way to the end. Now she sang it before eating and after the toilet too. The sun came in the window. Iris held up her hands. They were smart, clean hands, and they smelled like flowers.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Henry sat in his car seat. The sun was hot on his arm. "I am hot," he said. "Can I have cold air?"

Mom drove up a big hill. The car went slow. Henry rolled down his window a little. The air was warm.

Then they went down the hill. The road went flat. Mom made the car go fast. Wind came in the window. The wind was cool on Henry's arm. It felt like cold air.

"The fast car makes wind," said Henry. "The wind makes me cool." He put his hand out a little bit. The wind pushed on his hand. When the car went slow, the wind stopped. When the car went fast, the wind came back. Henry made his hand go in and out, in and out.

A big truck went by. It was bigger than their car. A little blue car went by too. It was smaller. Henry waved at the little car.

At the ice cream shop, Mom had to pay. She gave coins to the man. The man gave Henry a cold ice cream. It was cold like the wind from the window. Henry licked it and smiled.

"I like fast cars," said Henry. "They make wind for me."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Daniel went to the park with Grandma. He wanted to find the ducks. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Daniel held her hand.

They passed a big grill by the picnic tables. It was smoking. Daniel reached out one finger. The air above the grill felt hot on his skin. He pulled his finger back fast. "Hot," said Daniel. Grandma nodded. "The grill is hot, so we do not touch it." Daniel put his hands in his pockets. That was a good plan.

Then they heard a splash. The ducks were in the pond! Daniel ran, but he stopped and looked back. He waited for Grandma. They walked to the water together. Daniel took off one shoe and put in one toe. The water was cold. "Brrr!" he said. The sun was going down. It was getting late. "The ducks go home when it gets late," said Grandma. Daniel waved. "Bye, ducks. See you next time."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Jake had a cold. He was resting in his big bed. His nose was red and dry. He wanted water, but the cup was empty.

Mom filled the cup up. She put it on the little table. Jake drank and drank. Soon his nose felt better. His throat did not hurt. "Why did water help?" Jake asked. Mom said, "Water helps a sick body."

Jake wanted to see if it was true. He drank more water before his nap. He woke up and his nose was soft again. "The water fixes my nose!" he said. He hugged his teddy bear, who was feeling shy in the corner. Jake smiled. He put his shoe by the door so he could play outside tomorrow. Then he drank one more sip. "Good night, cup," he whispered.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story: Grayson found a big box behind the couch. He climbed inside it. The box smelled like cardboard and old crayons. "This is my house," he said. He knocked on the wall. Knock, knock. His toy bear sat all alone in the corner. The bear was cold, Grayson thought. Bears need blankets. He wrapped the bear in a soft towel. Then he gave the bear a pretend drink from an empty cup. "Drink your milk," said Grayson. The bear tipped over. "Oh no!" said Grayson. "Are you sick?" He thought hard. "Yes. You need a boot." He put his rain boot next to the bear like a bed. He tapped the boot three times. "That is my magic spell," he whispered. The bear sat up tall. Grayson clapped. "The spell worked because I tapped three times," he said. "More milk, bear?"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pink pencil and white paper. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He squeezed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed down hard. The pencil tip went through the paper. "Oh no!" said Gabriel. "The paper did rip!"

A woman came to the table. It was Grandma. She held up her own hand. "Look at my fingers," she said. Gabriel looked. Grandma pinched the pencil with two fingers, like a little crab. Gabriel tried it too. He pinched the pencil with his thumb and one finger. He made the letter G. He made an A. He made a B! The paper did not rip. The letters were wiggly, but they were there.

"Grandma, look!" said Gabriel. "When I pinch soft, the paper stays good." He wrote his whole name, all the way to the last L. "G-A-B-R-I-E-L!" he shouted. "Now I can write it again!" And he pulled a new piece of paper close.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Bennett stood in the music room. His teacher sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Bennett clapped fast, fast, fast. Then he forgot the words. The song fell all apart.

His friend Mia showed him the big yellow drum. "Try this," she said. The drum went boom, boom, boom. It was slow and even, like a clock. Bennett clapped boom, boom, boom too. He did not clap fast this time. His claps fit right into the song. "My claps go with the drum," said Bennett. "The drum keeps them steady."

Now the teacher hid the paper with the words on it. Bennett closed his eyes. He thought of stars. He sang every word. Then he drank his milk and smiled. "Again!" he said.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Oliver sat at the dinner table. He wanted his brown bread before dinner. "Can I have bread?" he asked. Mom said, "First we count the beans."

Oliver looked at his plate. He did not know where to start. So he sang his counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The words came out in a long line, like a train.

He pointed at a bean and said, "One." He pointed again. "Two." The words went in the same order as the song. "Three, four, five." He counted five beans.

"Where did the words go after five?" he asked. He sang the song again, slow. Then he knew. "The song gives them to me in order," he said.

Mom smiled. "Now fetch the bread basket, please."

Oliver carried it back, one hand on each side. "One basket," he said, "and it is for me."

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Evan wanted a picnic in the backyard. He got his basket and his red trike. He would ride the trike to the big tree.

First he went to his little desk. Mom kept the picnic things there. He put in one apple. He put in one banana. He put in one cracker. Apples, bananas and crackers are foods. Foods go in a picnic basket.

Then he saw his blue ball. The ball went in too. Then his toy duck went in. Then his drum went in. The basket got very full. It was too heavy to ride with.

Buster the dog ran up. He sniffed the basket. He barked and barked. Evan thought about it. Buster did not bark at the ball. He did not bark at the duck. He barked at the apple. "Buster smells the food," said Evan. Dogs like to smell foods.

So Evan took out the toys. He rolled the ball under the tree. He set the duck on the grass. He kept the foods in the basket. Now the basket was light. Evan rode his trike to the tree.

He sat and ate his favorite apple. Buster sat with him. "One apple, one banana, one cracker," said Evan. Buster wagged his tail and got a tiny bite.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Isabelle went to the farm with her grandma. Grandma had a gift in her bag. It was a shiny little bell. Grandma hid it behind the hay.

"Find the bell," said Grandma. Isabelle looked at the cows. She looked at the hens. No bell yet. So Isabelle used her eyes to look. "My eyes find things," she said. Then she saw something shiny by the red boot. "The bell! My eyes found it."

Grandma rang the bell. Ding, ding! "My ears heard it," said Isabelle. She covered her ears. The sound went away. She took her hands off. Ding! The sound came back. "My ears hear sounds," she said.

Then Grandma held out fresh bread. Farmer Joe had begun to bake it that morning. Isabelle smelled it with her nose. "My nose smells bread," she said. She touched the soft bread with her fingers. "My fingers feel soft." She took a little bite. "My tongue tastes it. Yum!"

A small goat walked up. It nibbled Isabelle's hair. Isabelle laughed. "Goat, that is my hair!" The goat blinked at her. Grandma laughed too. Ding, ding, went the shiny bell.
